rationale: A wins because it mostly stays inside the facts and turns them into usable reporter shapes: “Allbirds is closing its own stores and signing a wholesale deal in the same breath” is a clean contradiction a retail trade reporter could actually use. B has sharper questions, but it keeps stepping onto unsupported trapdoors like “A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale.” Clever is not a substitute for sourced.
gaps_in_A: “latest sign DTC brands are shrinking to survive” overclaims a sector trend from one Allbirds update; the angle asks for comparables later, but the headline has already spent proof it does not have.
“brands are choosing fewer, better bets over growth-at-all-costs” is plausible retail-analysis language, not a supplied fact. Fine as a hypothesis, sloppy as stated fact.

“will finally make its shoes last” pushes past “more durable than its original wool runner” and implies the old shoe failed durability. That needs testing or customer evidence before it belongs in a headline.
gaps_in_B: “A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale” is invented. The update gives a wholesale partnership, not a decade-long anti-wholesale history.

“That’s a company publicly conceding its signature product had a durability problem” overstates the supplied fact. “More durable” is not automatically a confession; that’s the kind of flourish that gets a founder embarrassed on the first follow-up.
“the collapse of the direct-to-consumer orthodoxy and the return of brands to third-party shelves” imports a whole trend argument without evidence in the update.

“a shoe replaced twice as often is worse regardless of its carbon footprint” may be a smart sustainability thesis, but the update gives no lifecycle data, replacement-rate data, or executive willing to say it. B knows this, then pitches it anyway.
